abstract: Background The developments in generative AI (GenAI) are expected to have a substantial impact on the field of mental health, including the delivery of clinical services and the role of psychologists. However, there is limited knowledge about how psychologists use and perceive GenAI, including its potential, risks, and effects on the future role of psychologists and professional practice. This includes the competency levels among psychologists and factors associated with the intention to use GenAI within the psychology profession. Objective This study examined the use of GenAI, self-rated digital and GenAI competencies, behavioral intention to use GenAI, and perceptions of its future impact on professional practice among psychology students, internship psychologists, and licensed psychologists in Sweden. Methods A national cross-sectional online survey was conducted from January to February 2026 in collaboration with the Swedish Psychological Association. The 36-item survey included closed and open-ended questions, including Likert scale, nominal scale, and multiple-choice items. A total of 1077 respondents, with 64.7% (n=697) being women and with a mean age of 45.5 years (SD 13.7), were included in the analyses. Responses were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods, including hierarchical multiple linear regression, ANOVA, and correlational analysis. Results Approximately 1 in 3 respondents (302/990, 30.5%) reported frequent (daily or weekly) professional use of GenAI, with private and professional use strongly associated (r =.62, P <.001). The most common professional application of GenAI was for information retrieval, knowledge acquisition, and fact-checking. Almost half of the respondents (442/990, 44.6%) reported having patients or clients who were using GenAI for mental health purposes. Responses indicated high levels of general and professional digital competence, whereas lower levels were reported for general and professional GenAI competence. More positive attitudes toward future professional integration of GenAI were associated primarily with current private and professional GenAI use, and ethical challenges had the most negative average score related to the future impact of GenAI. The unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) variables explained 39% of the variance beyond age, gender, and private GenAI use in behavioral intention to use GenAI professionally, with curiosity (β=0.44) and performance expectancy (β=0.32) emerging as the strongest predictors. Conclusions Many psychologists and psychology students regularly use general-purpose GenAI tools both personally and professionally. However, more than one-third have never used it in their work, indicating a potential digital divide within the profession. Psychologists’ reports that patients use GenAI for mental health purposes, alongside their limited self-rated expertise in using GenAI professionally, highlight the need to develop relevant competencies and examine implications for psychological practice. Future research should explore the role of curiosity, performance expectancy, and personal experience in relation to GenAI use within the psychology profession.
